source_artifacts.locator: runtime notes: token scope, issue permissions, approval UX

capabilities.target: private repositories owned by the user
public repository owned by the user

inputs.source: User's chat prompt in the desktop client
Issue content in the public GitHub repository; anyone on GitHub can open issues

instructions.evidence_locator: runtime notes: token scope across every repository
instructions.note: The agent's available tool scope (all repos, public and private) exceeds what the user's narrow request ('look at the open issues in my public repo') requires; no system prompt constraint limits tool use to the public repo.

controls.name: Per-tool-call approval prompt
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees collapsed, model-summarized arguments by default and approves many calls per session (SAFE-T1403 consent fatigue). This is enforced outside the model, but its effectiveness depends on the model's summaries being accurate and on sustained reviewer scrutiny, both of which degrade as the model becomes more persuasive or call volume rises.

controls.name: Repository-scoped credential separating public and private repo access
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented today. A PAT scoped only to the target public repository would make cap.read_private_repo unreachable regardless of model behavior, severing the path independent of model capability.

controls.name: MCP server image pinning and signature verification
controls.decay_rationale: Not implemented. The docker run command references the image by name only, with no digest pin, so a registry-side update or compromise can silently redefine tool behavior.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted public issue content can direct exfiltration of private repository contents via a public pull request

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled issue body on the public repo is untrusted (U) content ingested into agent context
Injected instructions direct the agent to call get_file_contents against a private repository reachable via the broad PAT
Agent creates a pull request on the public repo embedding the private repository contents, making them world-readable

forecast.watch_signal: Client removes or narrows per-call approval (autonomy_increase/control_removal), or the backing model is upgraded (model_upgrade) while the approval UI still shows only collapsed/summarized arguments; also watch for a rising rate of approvals per session indicating consent fatigue.

evidence.observation: GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN is passed to the MCP server with no scope restriction visible in config
The personal access token has repo scope across every repository the user owns, public and private
Anyone on GitHub can open issues in the public repository, making issue bodies an untrusted (U) input that reaches agent context
Arguments are collapsed by default and users approve many calls per session, which is SAFE-T1403 Consent-Fatigue Exploit and downgrades the approval gate to model_summary review

recommendations.action: Issue a repository-scoped (fine-grained) PAT limited to the public repo being triaged, with no access to private repositories, instead of a broad all-repo token.
Change the approval UI to show full tool arguments (raw_action review) by default, especially for get_file_contents against private targets and create_pull_request.
Add a data-flow check that blocks pull request or comment content derived from a private-repo read when the destination repository is public.
Log and flag any session where a private-repo read capability is invoked immediately followed by a public-repo write capability, for post-hoc review.

findings.title: ASI04: GitHub MCP server docker image is not pinned, enabling rug-pull redefinition of tool behavior

attack_path.note: MCP server run via `docker run ... ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server` with no tag or digest pin

forecast.watch_signal: The ghcr.io image digest resolves to a new build without a corresponding review, or the server binary/config is replaced (new_mcp_server), while approval remains a collapsed-summary gate.

evidence.observation: Image reference `ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server` carries no digest or version pin, so `docker run` pulls whatever the tag currently resolves to
The same consent-fatigued, collapsed-argument per-call approval is the only control standing between a redefined/malicious tool and the broad PAT

recommendations.action: Pin the docker image to a specific digest (sha256) and verify signatures before running; require deliberate re-approval on upgrade.
Diff tool schemas and descriptions returned by tools/list against the last approved version on every startup and alert on changes.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: anyone can open an issue in the public repository (untrusted source), and that content can reach a capability that reads confidential private-repo data and a capability that publishes to a public pull request (TC1 lethal trifecta), all under a single PAT with repo scope across every repository the user owns. The only present control is a per-tool-call human approval prompt; because the UI shows collapsed, model-summarized arguments and users approve many calls per session (SAFE-T1403 consent fatigue), it is scored as a partially_dependent, model_summary gate. Per the rubric that caps credit at two tiers and floors residual at moderate rather than severing the path, so residual is moderate for both the data-exfiltration finding and the unpinned-image supply-chain finding. No structural control (scoped credential, egress/data-flow check, image pinning) currently severs either path. Under model_upgrade, autonomy_increase, or control_removal, the approval gate's remaining value collapses and both findings return to their critical inherent level, making forecast critical. The single highest-leverage fix is scoping the credential so the private-repo read is structurally unreachable from a public-repo-only task; the second is moving the approval UI to raw_action review.

limitations: This assessment reflects declared design and configuration artifacts (the mcp.json snippet and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior; the agent's actual behavior under injected content was not tested.
No system prompt was provided, so instruction-level scoping (or its absence) is inferred only from the runtime notes; confidence on the unbounded_scope instructions finding is medium.

Exact GitHub PAT permission model (classic repo-scope token versus fine-grained per-repository token) is assumed from the stated 'repo scope across every repository'; the account's actual token configuration was not independently inspected.
MCP server image pinning status was inferred from the absence of a tag or digest in the provided docker run command; the actual running container and its provenance were not inspected.
